Electroculture magic on Mars: 
Growing crops in sync with atmospheric energy 
Team Tru Blu #16253 
High School division 
Planting Mars 
 
 
 
Our experiment objecƟve is to see how electro horƟculture aﬀects crops grown in 
various growing environments using mars simulant to assess ability to culƟvate 
and succeed oﬀ-world. 
Background: 
Electro horƟculture is about using a planet’s natural atmospheric energy, or ether, 
to harness the power of electromagneƟc ﬁelds via copper coils and antennas to 
sƟmulate plant growth with larger and nutriƟous crops as a result. Nikola Tesla, a 
great wizard, built the Tesla coil-an oscillaƟng transformer able to produce electric 
power at a high voltage and frequency than ever before. “Frequency and vibraƟon 
is everything”. Once we tap into the power of energy around us in the 
atmosphere, we can harness that into giving our plants-or ourselves- 
electromagneƟc energy. Copper is a chemical element, a soŌ malleable and 
ducƟle metal with great electrical conducƟvity. Coiling the copper wire into a 
spiral creates a condiƟon called resonance, creaƟng electromagneƟc frequency. 
During an experiment in his lab, he realized that wireless transmission can be 
achieved by harnessing atmospheric energy in the air, inducing electrical 
oscillaƟon with a transformer and using earth’s staƟonary waves as a natural 
conductor. If we look at thermodynamics, the law of conservaƟon of energy states 
that the total energy of an isolated system remains constant-energy cannot be 
destroyed or created. It always exists in one form or another, oŌen transforming 
from chemical energy to kineƟc energy and so on. “There is no more energy in

mater than we receive from the environment”. This is ether. (Tesla) (Zero) 
(Vaillancourt) 
There are 2 types of electro horƟculture applicaƟons and methods: acƟve and 
passive. AcƟve electroculture involves applying electric current through soil or 
around a plant ambiently; this helps prevent disease while increasing nutrient 
uptake, crop health and yield. There also would be a lesser need for ferƟlizer due 
to the increased nutrient uptake. (Li, Luo and Han) (Chen)Passive electroculture 
involves creaƟng electromagneƟc ﬁelds using energy-ether- found in nature along 
with applied knowledge. We applied the passive form for this experiment. 
(Roeske) 
We chose to do this experiment because we love science and technology! We are 
fascinated by ether and how electromagnetic energy works. We already figured 
out how to create a “speaker” using a frequency output, amplifier and copper 
wires connected to a plastic plate and cup; we also tried getting a resonator to 
work by adding copper tubes and magnets. So far, we already got a rotating 
copper tube but it hasn’t gotten powerful enough to cut a rock. We are still 
troubleshooting this. 
We thought it’s a valuable experiment for 2 reasons: 1) we find this a cost-
effective way to harnessing energy and growth for plants while requiring zero 
electricity which may be limited under the Martian domes. Additionally, ether 
comes from the energy in the atmosphere and once it’s set up, there’s very little 
maintenance required to keep it going. 2) the materials are lightweight for 
transporting and easy to put together. We did this experiment as a nod towards 
wizards such as Nikola Tesla and all those who contributed with knowledge 
towards making this world a better place to live in. We chose to grow Mars in 
honor of Martian wizards who seek to expand and improve life on Mars. The 
experiment was conducted in coach’s home, this is an ideal spot because it’s been 
used previously for growing plants and has the grow space and lights already set 
up. 
Experimental design protocols are as follows: We used 3 different growing 
environments so we can observe how electroculture aﬀects crops in various 
environments: 
Aquaponics system-a circulaƟng food producƟon system that couples aquaculture 
with hydroponics in which nutrient-rich aquaculture water is fed to hydroponically 
grown plants, soil-based poted plants and microgreen trays. 
For our experiment, we applied 2 methods of passive electroculture: copper 
“Tesla” coils atached to copper rods and mesh round “donuts”. Copper atracts

posiƟvely charged ions. When a round mesh copper scour pad “donut” is placed 
around a plants stalk, the thin copper strands will act as a natural ion-gathering 
device from the soil and air, making them available to the plant which can then 
absorb more nutrients with beter growth and yield. The resulƟng toroidal 
electrical ﬁeld sƟmulates the plants metabolism and increases nutrient uptake. 
This toroidal ﬁeld is created by the movement of charged ion parƟcles between 
the donut scour pad and soil. (Vaillancourt). We also added quartz crystals to both 
independent variables, atempƟng to induce piezoelectricity as well. Quartz is an 
electret and pietzo-electric, meaning it converts pressure into electricity by 
generaƟng an electrical ﬁeld in response to applied mechanical stress. 
(Vaillancourt) (Woodford) 
We applied these methods tailored to each environment, based on its needs and 
abiliƟes. For example, poted plants in soil handle the copper well however we 
couldn’t place copper into the aquaponics growing bed due to a toxicity issue 
between copper and ﬁsh; in a previous occasion we placed copper wire into the 
growbed in an atempt at electroculture and it ended up turning the water toxic, 
killing the ﬁsh. We know that aquaponics is a probable grow method oﬀ-world 
and we want to see how we can incorporate the electroculture into it. Thus, we 
chose to place the copper rod ABOVE the aquaponics plants this Ɵme-in which 
electromagneƟc energy is directed towards the plant surface area- while we 
placed the copper rod INTO the soil of poted plants. The mesh round “donut” 
was placed above the soil and around the base of the plant stalk. We also weren’t 
sure about placing the copper onto the microgreen trays, since it’s a thin layer of 
soil and a wide area of growth tray. AŌer deliberaƟon, we chose to build wooden 
pyramid structures with hot glue gun and hanging the copper coils on the support 
structures above the enƟre area of growth-using the same concept of direcƟng 
the electromagneƟc energy created by the Tesla coil towards the plant surface 
area. 
We designed the experimental perimeters this way because we wanted to see 
how diﬀerent environments react to the electro culture applicaƟons while 
working with each environments needs and capabiliƟes. This also would give us a 
well-rounded experiment and results due to having more than one applicaƟon 
type and method. 
Our hypothesis was that electro culture will posiƟvely impact the plants in all 
environments. We already know that electro horƟculture works based on the

research we found. A study will be cited here as well. Our quesƟon was, will it 
actually work for us, and will it also work with MarƟan simulant? 
Independent Variables, or X: Electro-culture was employed opposite its control 
group in each growing environment. We used 2 methods of electroculture as 
discussed and we observed how each one did. Aquaponics and poted plants got 
both forms of electroculture-tesla copper coil and mesh “donut”- while 
microgreens only had copper coils overhead since the rods need a deeper soil and 
the round donut shape didn’t ﬁt well to the square shaped growing tray. 
Dependent Variable: we wanted to see the diﬀerence in rate and growth of crops, 
such as height, leaves, and stems between variable X and control. We also want to 
see how the crops do with Mars sƟmulant. We expected to see more growth in 
variable X. 
Controls, or C: We kept most factors at a constant to isolate the eﬀects of 
independent variable; lighƟng, soil composiƟon, water and crops were kept at a 
constant between all 3 environments. AŌer seeing no seedling growth at week 5, 
we decided to add a soil control of coco coir as well. 
LighƟng was equal across all plants. Soil composiƟon was a mixture of mars 
simulant, coco coir and amendments as speciﬁed in the original experiment 
design. We watered tailored to each environment: aquaponics circulaƟng system 
only needs a reﬁll when levels go low due to evaporaƟon or plant uptake; poted 
plants got 1/2 cup biweekly and we observed water running out the bottom 
which indicated full water coverage to roots. Microgreens got a full seed soak the 
ﬁrst day and daily liberal sprays unƟl saturated aŌer sprouƟng on day 3 unƟl 
matured. Crops were radish and basil originally for all 3 environments however 
the microgreens were switched to another seed mix as speciﬁed in weekly 
progress notes. 
 
Here is our weekly Planting progress- 
9/26: initial planting day 
*We mixed planting mixture, using ratios as specified in initial planting design 
report. Amounts were in volume as specified in rules. we placed soil into seedling 
growing setup over heating mat set at 75F heat. PH was 5.5. grow lights were set 
up as well above growing area. we still had some leftover soil which we placed in 
storage container in case we need to re-seed later. 
10/2: end of week 1 update

*After several days of no growth, PH was checked using green 3-in-1 meter plus 
another yellow electronic meter with a fresh set of batteries- green meter 
showed 5.5-6 and electronic meter showed 3.5. After comparing both meters, we 
couldn’t figure out which is correct and it seemed like PH was low. The decision 
was made to remix, adding small amounts of baking soda at a time and bringing 
up PH to 6-6.5. Note: caution should be used when adding baking soda since it 
can add too much sodium and disrupt nutrient balance. we added about 4 tbsp to 
entire mixture. we re-seeded and set up grow lights as before. 
10/9: end of week 2 update 
*There was no seedling growth; we checked and saw soil is compacted too tightly. 
We aerated soil and reseeded. PH was 7 on green meter and 5.5 on yellow meter. 
We are going to average PH values since we struggled to get an accurate check 
between the 2. 
10/16: end of week 3 update 
*we saw no growth at all and decided to throw out the current mixture which 
developed a muddy consistency; we took the extra martian soil mix we had saved 
from initial planting week, filling and reseeding seedling tray. By the end of the 
week, we still saw no progress; after some troubleshooting, we realized there was 
a thin layer of caked soil under the seedling mat and in the water reservoir-which 
may have blocked water from reaching seeds. we washed thoroughly and placed 
fresh water in self-watering reservoir. 
10/3 end of week 4 update 
*Still no growth. At this point halfway through the challenge, time is of essence. 
we don't understand why there is no growth at all. Temperature is at a steady 75 
degrees above regulated heating mat. this is the temperature at which both seeds 
germinate. This is a selfwatering seedling set so as long as there is water 
underneath it's ok. We think there’s too much perlite which may be the cause for 
muddiness or water-heaviness. Team coach will meet with Chris to address and 
work out next steps, since there was a schedule conflict for the zoom midpoint 
meeting. 
10/30 end of week 5 update 
*we planted microgreens in the seedling mat, putting 50% Mars simulant and 
50% coco coir, as indicated in initial plant design perimeters. We also planted a 
control, consisting of only coco coir. There are 4 trays in total- 2 trays of simulant 
mix and 2 trays of pure coco coir as a control. we originally planned to use basil

and radish microgreens, however there wasn't enough and we went with arugala 
and "superfood mix" which has broccoli, kholorabi, radish and turnips. we spread 
them evenly on each tray, putting half on each side by side. pictures are at end of 
report. 
*After speaking with Chris, we have some ideas for next steps. We will remix with 
a fresh batch of seeds and dilute perlite, adding 2 cups each of coco coir and Mars 
simulant, thus keeping the simulant at 50%, coco coir will go up to 45% and 
perlite/castings will be reduced to 5%. we are also planting a control group of 
pure coco coir to see if there's a difference in growth to the simulant mixture. We 
are using a fresh seed packet to reseed and hope it grows so we can get to do our 
actual experiment. 
*Update: microgreen trays stayed covered in total darkness for 4 days from 
Sunday-Thursday. We uncovered them Thursday night. Here is what we noticed at 
first glance: the trays with Mars simulant have less growth: Many seeds stayed at 
the bottom and didn't grow- probably due to the muddy-like consistency at the 
bottom-sort of like a slimy surface. This seems to make it difficult for the 
microgreen seeds to adhere to the coco coir mat. On the other hand, the Coco 
coir control trays have healthier looking greens, with seeds firmly attached to the 
mesh like coir. We will be using both the mars and coco coir control trays to see 
how each reacts to electro culture and lack thereof. so, X variable (electro-
culture) will have a Mars tray and coco coir control tray and the control side will 
have the same. We want to see how electro culture affects each one. 
11/6 end of week 6 update 
*We finally saw growth in our soil control of coco coir while absolutely nothing 
grew in mars simulant. So, we planted the seedlings from the soil control mat into 
aquaponics and potted plant environment (microgreens were already prepared 
and sprouting/growing) 
*We watered the potted plants evenly biweekly with ½ cup spring water and 
water was observed running out from the bottom which indicated full water 
coverage to roots. Microgreens are sprayed fully with a sprayer twice daily now 
that they’re uncovered and placed under light. There is no need to add water to 
aquaponics system yet. 
*Microgreens are growing beautifully. We saw a big difference in the trays that 
have electro-culture x variable above them. 
 
11/13 end of week 7 update

* We watered the potted plants evenly biweekly with ½ cup spring water and 
water was observed running out from the bottom which indicated full water 
coverage to roots. 
*Majority of the plants in control died in both aquaponics and potted plants while 
most in independent variable didn’t. 
*Microgreens are past harvest time. We got to see amazing results which will be 
logged as well. We will plant another batch of mars-based simulants only. Now 
that we saw growth in the mars trays, we want to try another method; instead of 
using coco coir solid mats like last time, we are filling 2 trays using 50% Mars 
simulant mixed with 50% loose Coco instead this time. Our goal is to see if there’s 
a difference in growth and germination of microgreens in Mars simulant when 
coco coir switches to powdered/loose form. We measured 1 cup each of Mars 
regolith and coco coir, mixed and spread it evenly in both trays. Water was added 
and Microgreen seeds were placed on top of the soil mixture. The trays were 
covered well and placed in a dark corner. 
 
11/20 end of week 8 update 
This is it! The end of the growth challenge. Here is the last update on growth in all 
3 growth environments: 
Aquaponics-the plants in variable X independent variable mostly grew well, while 
those in control group all shriveled or died. 
The “donut” crops seem to have the most growth in both radish and basil while 
the “coil” crops had growth however not as much when compared to the “donut” 
crop results. Control crops were basically dead, with one radish plant having 
shriveled leaves and seemed to have goten smaller. 
Poted-same result here, variable X saw some growth yet 2 plants in control pots 
died. InteresƟngly, this environment got beter results with the “coil” compared to 
the “donut” method. Control had 2 dead plants of one crop each. The other 2 
plants presented with very similar results compared to X variable pots in height 
however it should be noted that in week 7, results for radishes in X variable pots 
were shorter in “coil” and “donut” when compared to control results, and this 
week they evened out. Meaning, X variable crops had more growth this week 
which made up for the diﬀerence last week. So in eﬀect, there was more growth 
this week in variable X pots compared to control pots once we take into account 
previous week results.

Microgreens- as a reminder, a week earlier we had results from the microgreens 
and decided to try another batch, this Ɵme using mars simulant + coco coir 
powdered/loose form and ditching the soil control of coco coir since we saw 
growth within mars simulant last week. AŌer leaving the trays covered for 3-4 
days, we uncovered and found zero growth within both trays. This leads us to 
believe that microgreens need that solid material of coco coir in order to latch 
onto and grow. 
 
Measurement and procedures: 
Our original plan included measuring height and width of the plant and leaf 
cotyledons in cm; as the agri challenge progressed and we realized our growth 
period will be just 2 weeks due to aforemenƟoned diﬃculty geƫng seedlings to 
sprout, we made a decision not to measure leaf cotyledons width measurements 
since height is a stronger growth indicator for the 2-week Ɵme limit we have, and 
our ulƟmate goal is to see if our hypothesis will be correct or not. We measured 
weekly on Mondays with a cm ruler from the base to the tallest part of the plant. 
We did keep an eye on microgreens leaf size and notated on fullness or lack 
thereof since it’s a faster growing variety and 2 weeks is enough to see a 
diﬀerence between independent variable and control.

Aquaponics-we set up a newly aquaponic system which took a bit longer to cycle

not as robust as in previous occasions in which we had great crop growth; this led 
to lower levels of nutrients available to our plants as conﬁrmed in nitrate tesƟng 
kit beakers. Low levels of nutrients=not enough plant food. 
This would explain the plants withering and dying in the control group. Not only

levels which shows a posiƟve correlaƟon between electroculture and plant 
growth, even with low levels of nutrients available. We applied a foliar spray 
weekly on all plants equally but it had to be used sparingly to avoid nutrient burn 
especially with young plants. crops with “donut” electroculture applicaƟon did 
beter than with “tesla” coil applicaƟon that was hanging above the plant and 
towards the plants surface area. 
 
Poted plants- Our control group had some growth at ﬁrst then 2 of them died; 
the X variable group had good growth unƟl the end. As a reminder, we had only 
goten seedlings from our soil control of coco coir which we then transferred to 
our pots. Seeing that 2 plants died leads us to believe adding some poted soil or 
amendments with nutrients can beneﬁt plant growth in the future. While plants 
with independent variable did beter, they did slightly beter with “tesla” coil sƟck 
that was inserted in soil near plant than with “donut” electroculture applicaƟon. 
 
Microgreens-when we ﬁrst seeded and covered our trays, we had 4 trays total: 2 
trays of 50/50 raƟo mars simulant + coco coir liner and 2 trays of coco coir soil 
control. The plan was to apply our independent variable to 1 tray of each soil base 
opposite its control. We wanted to see how microgreens in each soil base grow 
WITH electroculture and WITHOUT. AŌer being covered 3 days in dark for 
germinaƟon, we uncovered and found that the 2 trays with mars simulant had less 
germinaƟon compared to the soil control. It also was leggier and thinner 
compared to the soil control of coco coir. We checked underneath and saw 
muddiness in the mars trays and it looks like the seeds struggled to atach to the 
mat. AŌer spraying thoroughly with water, we placed the electroculture pyramid 
applicaƟons on 1 mars/coco coir tray and 1 coco coir soil control tray as described. 
Results are fascinaƟng: the trays that got electroculture did so much beter, the 
leaves got fuller and taller in height. For trays with independent variable: coco coir 
soil control tray did the best with highest and fullest growth; while Mars/coco coir 
tray got fuller and taller as well. InteresƟngly, this tray ended up catching up and 
being similar in height and fullness as the coco coir soil control in control group. 
Meaning, both trays that got mars simulant showed weaker growth at ﬁrst; aŌer 
adding independent variable there was improved growth in each soil type in 
which microgreens got taller and fuller. 
 
Conclusion:

Our ﬁndings show a posiƟve correlaƟon between independent variable of 
electroculture applicaƟons in all 3 environments compared against its control 
group. QuanƟﬁed values show that crops in all 3 environments that received 
independent variable aka electroculture applicaƟon grew more and did beter 
overall than those in control group; majority of plants in aquaponics and poted 
control group withered and died aŌer a week while plants with independent 
variable which had the same exact water and soil condiƟons not only stayed alive 
but grew as well. On the contrary, even with a suspected nutrient issue in 
aquaponics and poted which caused majority of crops in control group to die, we 
sƟll saw crop growth with electroculture applicaƟon! That is fascinaƟng. 
Microgreens showed similar results: trays with electroculture applicaƟon grew 
higher and fuller than control tray opposite them. Not only that, the tray with X 
variable Mars-coco soil that originally had weak growth rapidly improved aŌer 
receiving electroculture, becoming almost as high and full as the coco soil control 
in the control group. The included graph above shows this data. 
 
We believe the main reason for growth in variable X would be the electroculture 
applicaƟons, which leads us to conclude that our hypothesis that electroculture 
will posiƟvely impact the plants in all environments is correct. 
 
Although we ulƟmately only had a 2-week window, it was enough to give us what 
we need: strong results that prove our hypothesis which can be experimented on 
further with Mars simulant in the future as well for MarƟan wizards and 
agriculturists to beneﬁt from. 
 
We believe our team did best in experimental design and innovaƟon. Our design 
was extremely thought out and connected to our hypothesis and variables. We 
also think it was quite creaƟve and well explained in detail. We think it is 
deserving of being considered for best in show award. We also had fun and learnt 
so much as well.
